newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GYPSIES ASK CANADIAN EMBASSIES ABOUT ASYLUM.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GYPSIES ASK CANADIAN EMBASSIES ABOUT ASYLUM.

text.p: Czech gypsies have flocked to Canadian embassies in Prague and Vienna hoping to win asylum after a local television report showed a gypsy family living comfortably in Canada while its case is considered.
The reaction to the report on the commercial station TV Nova last Thursday has grown into a heated debate in the media over attitudes toward the large Czech gypsy population.

Ottawa's Prague embassy said on Tuesday that it received several hundred calls since the report, mostly from Czech gypsies in the eastern city of Ostrava who mistakenly thought Canada has a special asylum programme for them.
The Czech news agency CTK reported from Ostrava that up to 5,000 gypsies had begun selling their posessions and drawing out money after the report to buy air tickets to Canada.

"(TV Nova) basically showed that if you arrive in Canada, from that moment, you get money from the government, they take care of your accommodation and your chances of getting refugee status or a job are very high...," Canada's Prague embassy spokewoman Lucie Cermakova told Reuters.
"But in fact it's a very complicated administrative process and you have to fulfil a lot of requirements."
Czech citizens are not required to have a visa to visit Canada although they must show a return ticket when entering and prove they have the means to finance their stay.

"People who visit Canada... who believe they cannot return home for reasons of persecution, have access to our Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB)," Jacques Beaulne, a counsellor at Canada's Vienna embassy who handles immigration services for the region, told Reuters.
"It does not apply to particular groups of people from particular places... It's there for people needing protection."
He stressed that there was no special programme for Czech gypsies, and that Canada's policy was consistent with all countries following the United Nations convention on refugees.
"Canada is not paradise... We are not going to let people starve, but people are not going to be able to benefit financially from such a situation," Beaulne said.

Czech politicians have long wrestled with accusations by human rights campaigners, and western governments, that the country unfairly treats its relatively poor gypsies, who are loosely estimated to total in the hundreds of thousands.
Cermakova said Canada's official position was that there was racism towards gypsies in Czech society but "it's not supported by the (Czech) government."
Czech Gypsies have often been the target of violent racially motivated attacks, and there is a widespread belief that they are responsible for much of the country's crime.
The Czech daily Mlada Fronta Dnes said on Tuesday that local officials in the Ostrava suburbs of Marianske Hory and Tachov were considering to buy tickets to Canada for gypsies.

"I see that two groups live here, romany (gypsies) and white, who do not fit together. They do not want to live together," mayor Liana Janackova, a member of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party, was quoted as saying.
The comment sparked a sharp response from President Vaclav Havel's office which labled the comments as racist.
"It's not racist, just the opposite. We want to help the romany," Janackova told Mlada Fronta.
CTK quoted an unnamed senior Czech minister as saying that he was "terrified" with the reaction to the TV Nova report which had started something "which could be very dangerous".
It said Klaus was expected to convene the government's council on national minorities to discuss the situation.
